lesson.title: Selectivity: Why a High Q Circuit Can Ignore Its Neighbors
lesson.summary: Selectivity describes how sharply a resonant circuit distinguishes its target frequency from nearby ones, rising with quality factor and falling with bandwidth.
lesson.body:
Selectivity describes how well a resonant circuit distinguishes the one frequency it is tuned to from frequencies nearby, and it is governed entirely by quality factor and bandwidth, the two ideas from the previous chapters. A highly selective circuit has a narrow bandwidth relative to its resonant frequency, meaning high Q, and its response falls off steeply for any frequency even a little off resonance. A poorly selective circuit has a wide bandwidth, low Q, and barely distinguishes the target frequency from its neighbors. This tradeoff is exactly what a radio tuner needs to solve: pull in one station and reject the next one over, which sits just a little higher or lower in frequency.

Compare two versions of the series RLC circuit used throughout this unit, both with L equals 1 H and C equals 1 microfarad, so both share the same resonant frequency, omega_0 equals 1000 rad/s. Circuit A keeps R equals 100 ohms, giving Q equals 10 and bandwidth equals omega_0 over Q equals 1000 over 10, which is 100 rad/s, matching the bandwidth chapter. Circuit B lowers the resistance to R equals 10 ohms, giving Q equals omega_0 L over R equals 1000 times 1 over 10, which is 100, ten times higher, and bandwidth equals omega_0 over Q equals 1000 over 100, which is only 10 rad/s, ten times narrower. Lower resistance means less energy lost per cycle, higher Q, and a tighter, more selective resonance peak.

To see the practical difference, check how each circuit responds to a signal 10 percent above resonance, at omega equals 1.1 times omega_0, or 1100 rad/s. The general shape of a series RLC response away from resonance is the magnitude of H equals 1 over the square root of 1 plus (Q times x) squared, where x equals omega over omega_0 minus omega_0 over omega. Here x equals 1.1 minus (1 over 1.1), which is 1.1 minus 0.9091, or 0.1909.

For Circuit A, Q times x equals 10 times 0.1909, which is 1.909. Squaring gives 3.645, adding 1 gives 4.645, and its square root is 2.155. The magnitude is 1 over 2.155, which is 0.464, or in decibels, about negative 6.67 dB. For Circuit B, Q times x equals 100 times 0.1909, which is 19.09. Squaring gives 364.5, adding 1 gives 365.5, and its square root is 19.12. The magnitude is 1 over 19.12, which is 0.0523, or in decibels, about negative 25.63 dB.

Ten percent off resonance, the low Q Circuit A has only quietly attenuated the unwanted frequency by 6.67 dB, while the high Q Circuit B has crushed it by 25.63 dB, nearly 19 dB more rejection from the same 10 percent detuning. That difference is what selectivity actually buys: the same nearby interfering signal that a low Q circuit lets leak through almost unharmed is nearly eliminated by a high Q circuit. The cost, as the bandwidth chapter would predict, is that Circuit B also has a much narrower usable passband, so a highly selective circuit is only a good choice when the signal of interest genuinely occupies a narrow slice of frequency.
